newsitem.title: USA: Albright vows to maintain pressure on Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Albright vows to maintain pressure on Cambodia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright vowed on Wednesday to maintain international pressure on Cambodian strongman Hun Sen to fulfil promises to accept mediation in Cambodia's crisis and restore coalition government there.

In a speech to the Los Angeles World Affairs Council, she also called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to play a greater role in Burma, saying that by admitting Burma as a member this year, "Burma's problems now become ASEAN's problems."

The comments were her most direct on Cambodia since Hun Sen seized sole power there in a military coup on July 6. Her words on Burma constituted a direct challenge to ASEAN as she heads for the group's annual meeting in Kuala Lumpur.
Albright noted that Hun Sen, who ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh as first prime minister, had initially rejected ASEAN's help in negotiating a solution to the crisis.

But she said that on Wednesday Hun Sen -- through his spokesman -- appeared to have accepted ASEAN's offer of mediation and promised to restore the previous coalition government and observe the rule of law.
"The United States will use its leverage and do all we can in partnership with others to see that Hun Sen's words are translated into concrete action," Albright said.
"This will be one of our primary goals at the (ASEAN) meetings this weekend in Kuala Lumpur," she said.
Albright complained that with the coup "democracy has taken a giant step backwards" in Cambodia and "dozens of people have reportedly been murdered."
She rejected Hun Sen's demand that other countries stop interfering in Cambodia's affairs.

The international community, which helped bring about Cambodia's fragile peace through a 1991 treaty and billions of dollars in aid, had a right to insist that Phnom Penh respect democratic principles, she said.

At ASEAN, "my purpose will be to maintain international pressure on Cambodian authorities to respect the 1991 Paris peace agreement, allow political parties to operate freely and prepare for fair elections next year," she said.

Albright pointedly did not call for Ranariddh's reinstatement, even though his royalist party won U.N.-monitored elections in 1993. U.S. officials privately acknowledge Ranariddh's return to power is most unlikely although they insist that his party be involved in government.
Unlike Cambodia, whose membership is on hold, ASEAN this year admitted Burma to its group despite U.S. disapproval.
President Bill Clinton in April imposed a ban on new U.S. investment in Burma, whose authorities Albright called "among the most repressive and intrusive on earth."
But U.S. friends and allies in ASEAN rejected that view, preferring dialogue with Burma's military junta.

Albright called Burma a "brake" on Southeast Asia's progress and said until the country moves toward democracy and respect for law "Burma may be inside ASEAN but it will remain outside the Southeast Asian mainstream."

"By admitting Burma as a member ASEAN assumes a greater responsibility: for Burma's problems now become ASEAN's problems. And the goal of democratic change and respect for human rights in Burma becomes not only a national but a regional and global imperative," Albright said.
She decreed herself optimistic about Vietnam's progress, saying it "still has a long way to go but (it) is a nation on the move and it is moving in the right direction."
